title: Deep learning-based gait analysis predicts multisystem health phenotypes
desc: Nature Medicine, Published online: 09 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41591-026-04725-8 We developed a gait foundation model from three-dimensional skeletal motion data of 3,328 deeply phenotyped adults, recorded using a depth camera during five motor tasks. Embeddings significantly predicted 1,887 of 3,210 phenotypic targets and provided predictive gains across all 18 body systems in men and 17 out of 18 in women, while also improving prediction of clinical diagnoses and medication use.

title: Artificial Intelligence Use in Interventional Clinical Trials Registered on ClinicalTrials.gov.
Artificial Intelligence in Pediatric Hospital Medicine: Foundations, Clinical Applications, and Emerging Case Uses.
desc: [Pediatric annals] Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming health care and has important implications for pediatric hospital medicine. Advances in machine learning and large language models have enabled applications that support patient care in the areas of clinical documentation, decision making, and prognostic modeling. Pediatric AI systems leverage diverse data sources, including electronic health records, medical imaging, physiologic monitoring, wearable devices, and genomic data. Current applications include AI-powered scribes, chart summarization, clinical decision support, prediction of sepsis and clinical deterioration, precision pharmacotherapy, rare disease diagnosis, and mental health interventions. These technologies have demonstrated potential to reduce clinician workload, enhance diagnostic accuracy, and facilitate earlier therapeutic interventions. However, significant challenges remain, including limited and heterogeneous pediatric datasets by virtue of age and developmental characteristics in children, bias, privacy concerns, lack of representativeness, and the need for rigorous validation and oversight. As AI adoption expands, pediatric hospitalists require foundational knowledge of AI principles and limitations to ensure safe, equitable, and effective implementation. With appropriate governance and multidisciplinary collaboration, AI has the potential to improve pediatric inpatient outcomes and health care delivery.

title: Predicting Benefit From Anthracycline-Free Adjuvant Chemotherapy in High-Risk HER2-Negative Breast Cancer
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Peking Union Medical College Hospital; conditions: Breast Neoplasms, HER2-negative Breast Cancer; type: OBSERVATIONAL; enrollment: 100; status: ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING] This is an observational cohort study. Investigators do not assign any intervention to participants. Chemotherapy was received in a completed clinical trial or is determined by the treating physicians as part of routine care, and study results will not be used to guide treatment. The study aims to identify clinicopathological and molecular features associated with outcomes after anthracycline-free or anthracycline-containing chemotherapy in women with high-risk, HER2-negative early breast cancer. Existing clinical and follow-up data and archived tumor tissue from participants of a trial completed at Peking Union Medical College Hospital (NCT01354522; enrollment ended in 2013) will be analyzed with gene expression, metabolic, and digital pathology methods to develop a prediction model. Tumor tissue remaining after routine surgery or biopsy will also be collected, with informed consent, from up to 50 additional patients for single-cell sequencing. All analyses are exploratory.

title: NPCBench: A Clinical Apprenticeship Benchmark for Multimodal Care-Pathway Reasoning in Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma
desc: Current medical benchmarks typically break down clinical competence into isolated factual questions, single-image tasks, or static case vignettes. These tests score individual answers, but reveal less about whether a model can integrate subspecialty knowledge with multimodal evidence and track a patient's condition throughout a course of care. To close this gap, we introduce NPCBench, a clinical apprenticeship benchmark for nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC). NPCBench mirrors specialist training, from guideline and foundational knowledge to case planning, longitudinal review, CarePath integration, and open-ended consultation. It contains 4,777 component and consultation items and a 100-patient CarePath cohort with 417 scored diagnostic and care tasks. The episode-level evaluation tests whether diagnostic and care answers are jointly correct within a care pathway. By linking stepwise tasks to patient-level care trajectories, NPCBench evaluates whether models ground decisions in visual evidence, interpret changes in patient state, and meet clinical requirements in consultation. Across 30 evaluated models, we observe a composition gap: strong performance on individual tasks does not ensure jointly correct diagnostic and care answers for the same patient. Among 21 multimodal models, strict CarePath success reaches at most 23%. Paired controls and physician calibration further examine evidence grounding, longitudinal revision, and consultation judging. Overall, NPCBench broadens the evaluation of medical artificial intelligence beyond static question-answering paradigms to an apprenticeship-oriented assessment of clinical workflows, thereby offering a testbed for evidence-based and temporally coherent reasoning in oncology care.

title: Randomized Trial Protocol: Head-to-Head Comparison of Two Ambient Artificial Intelligence Documentation Tools on Clinician Usability
desc: Abstract Background: Ambient AI documentation reduces documentation burden and electronic health record (EHR) time for ambulatory clinicians. Newer features also queue orders and offer some level of coding support for clinician review. This study compares two commercial products deployed at UCLA Health. Objective: To compare Nabla and Epic Systems, Inc. ambient AI solution among ambulatory clinicians at UCLA Health on usability, documentation burden, perceived note quality, adoption, EHR time and productivity, clinician-reported experience with order queueing and coding support, coding and billing patterns and integrity, work productivity, and patient-reported communication experience. Methods: Two-arm parallel-group randomized trial, 1:1, among 374 ambulatory clinicians at a single academic health system who hold an active license for a standalone ambient application (Nabla). Randomization is covariate-constrained where cohort size permits, balancing age, sex, half-day clinic sessions, specialty group, and baseline System Usability Scale (SUS) score. Intervention runs 11/9/2026 to 1/17/2027, with the first four weeks as lead-in. The primary outcome is SUS score at follow-up, compared between arms. Analysis is by intention-to-treat using mixed-effects models. Ethics and dissemination: Determined exempt by the UCLA Institutional Review Board (IRB-26-2147). Survey completion indicates consent. No patient-level data are collected. Findings will directly inform operational decision making and will be published regardless of direction.

title: AI in the Clinical Documentation Loop: Effects of LLM-Induced Note Bloat and Diagnostic Overcall on Downstream LLMs
desc: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to process medical records for healthcare tasks such as clinical documentation. Because these tools also generate documentation, the relationship is now bidirectional: models both read from and write to the record. Understanding how LLMs behave when reading records that already contain LLM-authored content is therefore critical for their safe deployment. In this study, we examine how LLM-authored content in the medical record affects downstream LLMs that read the same record. We consider two types of LLM-induced artifacts: bloat, in which LLM-generated summaries accumulate in the record and change the length and provenance of its content over time; and distortion, in which LLMs subtly alter clinical findings rather than fabricating facts outright. As a case of distortion, we study diagnostic overcall (documenting an unconfirmed differential diagnosis in the record) and test whether it propagates to the reader LLM's output. Across seven reader models from four families, we find evidence of both effects. First, LLM-generated summary notes modestly but consistently degraded downstream hospital-course generation compared with copy-forward and templated text of matched length. Second, injected overcalls reappeared in downstream outputs at rates that varied by reader model, without detectable changes in standard quality metrics. These findings show the need to monitor AI-generated content in medical records and to account for it when those records are later processed by AI.

title: AOPTK: Open-Source Software for AI-Assisted Toxicological Literature Analysis
desc: Motivation: Toxicologists today face a challenge: although vast amounts of data describing how chemicals affect human health are available across scientific publications and regulatory reports, much of this information remains underutilized because extracting and interpreting evidence across thousands of studies is impractical to perform manually. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), particularly in large language models (LLMs), provide new opportunities to automate toxicological literature analysis. Results: Herein, we present the Adverse Outcome Pathway Toolkit (AOPTK), an open-source Python package for AI-enhanced analysis of toxicological and biomedical literature. AOPTK supports (i) automated literature retrieval from databases such as PubMed Central and Europe PMC, (ii) direct processing of full-text articles in PDF format, and (iii) LLM-assisted analysis tools to identify chemicals and extract their relationships to biological effects under user-defined conditions. We demonstrate its utilities through a case-study identifying potential non-genotoxic carcinogens based on their ability to inhibit gap junction intercellular communication (GJIC). The LLM-enhanced analysis achieves 81% agreement with an expert-curated inhibitor list and 95% accuracy in predicting inhibition versus no inhibition when analysing the same subset of 86 publications. Automated retrieval and analysis of 1 124 publications from PubMed Central further demonstrated the feasibility of applying AOPTK to large-scale literature analyses. Availability: The package is developed open source on GitHub, disseminated through PyPI and Bioconda and releases are archived on Zenodo. Individual tools are available in the Galaxy platform for accessible data analysis with user-friendly, findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable (FAIR) and end-to-end workflows provided via WorkflowHub. The tools are available on usegalaxy.eu and usegalaxy.cz and are developed open source on GitHub.

Resistance exercise to attenuate lean mass loss during tirzepatide therapy for obesity: a randomized controlled trial
desc: Incretin mimetics as obesity therapy induce substantial weight and fat loss but also decrease lean soft tissue mass, possibly impairing skeletal muscle function. Here, in this two-arm randomized controlled trial of adding resistance exercise (REx) to tirzepatide (T), 120 adults with overweight or obesity were treated with tirzepatide and randomized to thrice-weekly resistance exercise training or usual activities for 40 weeks. Tirzepatide was safe, and most participants tolerated up-titration to 15 mg weekly. Adherence to resistance exercise was 91%. Weight loss achieved was similar (T = −22.61 kg, T+REx = −22.28 kg, P = 0.694). For primary outcomes, loss of total fat mass was similar (T = −17.19 kg, T+REx = −17.98 kg, P = 0.700; between-group difference = −0.77 kg, 95% confidence interval (CI): −2.14 kg to 0.60 kg), but resistance exercise reduced loss of total lean soft tissue mass (T = −4.67 kg, T+REx = −3.57 kg, P < 0.001; between-group difference = 1.09 kg, 95% CI: 0.43−1.75 kg). For related endpoints, resistance exercise reduced loss of appendicular lean soft tissue mass (T = −3.55 kg, T+REx = −2.92 kg, P < 0.001). Upper and lower body muscle strength decreased with tirzepatide (bench press −4.09 kg, lat pulldown −4.42 kg, knee extension −4.42 kg) but increased with T+REx (+4.68 kg, +8.58 kg, +5.88 kg, respectively, all P < 0.001 versus tirzepatide). In conclusion, resistance exercise training attenuated loss of total lean soft tissue mass, representing an effective adjunct to tirzepatide anti-obesity therapy. Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry identifier: ACTRN12623001236684.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Pediatric Hospital Medicine: Governance, Ethics, Education, Research, and the Future Workforce.
desc: [Pediatric annals] Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly influencing pediatric inpatient care, extending beyond clinical applications to many areas of health care delivery, medical education, and research. Studies suggest that families are receptive to AI-assisted care if transparency, human oversight, and shared decision making are maintained. Effective governance is necessary to address concerns related to accountability, privacy, regulatory gaps, postdeployment monitoring, and equitable implementation. Algorithmic bias, data representativeness, informed consent, and the potential for AI to exacerbate health care disparities pose new ethical concerns. Explainable AI may improve transparency, trust, and acceptance by clinicians through making AI-generated recommendations more understandable. AI can also transform medical education through personalized learning, simulation, and clinical decision support, while requiring new competencies in AI literacy. AI offers opportunities to expedite clinical trials and data analysis but requires pediatric-specific frameworks to address age-related bias and emphasize ethical use of pediatric data in research. Responsible implementation, strong oversight, multidisciplinary collaboration, and continued clinician leadership will be essential to realizing AI's potential while safeguarding the welfare of pediatric patients and their families.

title: AI-Based Tools for Stroke Diagnosis, Treatment and Outcome Prediction: a Multicentre Prospective Observational Study
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Hospital Universitari Vall d'Hebron Research Institute; conditions: Stroke, Ischemic Stroke, Intracerebral Hemorrhage, Transient Ischemic Attack, Atrial Fibrillation; type: OBSERVATIONAL; enrollment: 10000; status: RECRUITING] Stroke is a leading cause of death and adult disability. Stroke care is still limited by fragmented care pathways, non-standardised diagnostic work-up and follow-up, and local, non-interoperable data systems across the pre-hospital, in-hospital and post-hospital settings. UMBRELLA-P is a multicentre, prospective, observational study in 7 university hospitals in 6 European countries (Spain, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands, Germany and Switzerland). Adults with clinically suspected acute stroke or transient ischemic attack (TIA) are managed according to standard of care. Routine clinical, imaging, laboratory, ECG and patient-reported data are collected, pseudonymised, stored on a dedicated server at each hospital and harmonised to the OMOP Common Data Model. The harmonised data form a federated real-world data platform (U-Platform). On this platform, artificial intelligence (AI) models are trained and validated through federated learning, so that no patient data leave the participating sites. The models aim to predict short- and long-term outcomes, reduce time to treatment, and support diagnosis, triage, discharge, follow-up and secondary prevention. Five clinical sub-studies address pre-hospital triage, fast track to reperfusion, emergent intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) management, TIA/minor stroke, and cardiac evaluation with blood biomarkers. The study is observational. The outputs of the AI models are used for research only and will not influence clinical decisions. Participants are followed for up to 12 months.

title: Multi-Agent Generative Artificial Intelligence for Transfusion Reaction Feature Extraction
desc: BACKGROUND: Many transfusion reactions are not reported to hemovigilance systems, and the features needed to recognize them are often documented only in free-text clinical notes. We sought to develop and evaluate an open-source, multi-agent artificial intelligence (AI) pipeline to extract transfusion reaction features defined by the National Healthcare Safety Network (NHSN) Hemovigilance Module from clinical notes. METHODS: We curated 181 features from the NHSN protocol and developed a multi-stage pipeline that extracted features, their timing, and clinical details from free-text notes. Three open-weight large language models (Qwen 3.6-27B, GPT-OSS-120B, and Kimi K3) were applied to 50 notes from expert-written scenarios, published case reports, and MIMIC-IV discharge summaries. Two physicians independently evaluated every model output in a blinded interface. The primary analysis was restricted to feature occurrences with concordant physician assessments. RESULTS: Physicians agreed on 1,201 of 1,343 co-rated feature occurrences (89.4%; Krippendorff's alpha 0.73). Precision was above 0.98 for all models. Sensitivity was 0.774 (95% CI 0.745-0.800) for Kimi K3, 0.636 (0.604-0.667) for GPT-OSS-120B, and 0.624 (0.593-0.655) for Qwen 3.6-27B, and specificity ranged from 0.952 to 0.991. Omissions accounted for more than 94% of false negatives. Timing and clinical details were judged supported or reasonable in more than 92% and 97% of assessments, respectively. Results were consistent across note sources and in analyses including discordant assessments. CONCLUSION: Multi-agent AI pipelines provide a feasible method for extracting transfusion reaction signals from clinical notes with high precision. Our work may have applications in active hemovigilance, reaction classification, and big data research.

title: Can General-Purpose Generative AI Supply Training Data for Medical Vision Models? A Multimodal Retrospective Study
desc: Background: Well-annotated, diverse medical imaging datasets remain a major constraint for vision-based medical AI. We evaluated Nano Banana, a general-purpose image generation and editing model, as a source of synthetic medical images for model training, subgroup augmentation, and model auditing. Methods: In this retrospective study across four imaging modalities, chest radiography, fundus photography, and CT models were trained only on synthetic images and externally validated on real-world data against real-data-trained models. Carotid ultrasound models were trained on a private Human Phenotype Project cohort (aged 40-75 years) with and without synthetic augmentation. Clinicians rated image plausibility. Evaluation used AUROC, AUPR, calibration, and decision curve analysis. Findings: Synthetic-only models achieved AUROCs of 0.877 (95% CI 0.843-0.910) for pneumonia (n=14863), 0.963 (0.948-0.975) for retinal detachment (n=1149), and 0.711 (0.600-0.823) for renal calculus (n=4122), comparable to real-data-trained models, but their calibration and net benefit were not consistently more favorable. With mixed synthetic-real training, a carotid ultrasound model produced an ordinal vascular age index that stratified 633 external subjects into subgroups differing in BMI and glucose (both p<0.01), linking vascular aging to cardiometabolic health. To stress-test shortcut learning, editing a moderate tessellated pattern into fundus photographs reduced the true-class probability for central serous chorioretinopathy from 0.996 to 0.822. Clinician-guided editing raised low-quality CT plausibility from 3.10/5 to 4.30/5. Interpretation: Synthetic data can complement real data in model training, subgroup representation, and model testing via controlled editing, but its clinical value should be assessed with calibration, decision curve analysis, and clinician review, not discrimination alone.
